analysis.one_liner: Bans toxic chemical flame retardants from children's products and furniture and directs safety regulators to study and restrict others.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban toxic flame retardants from children's products and furniture never got a hearing or a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited companies from making or selling children's products and upholstered furniture containing ten named chemical flame retardants, and required the Consumer Product Safety Commission to study all chemical flame retardants and ban any others that pose a substantial health risk [S2]. The reason anyone proposed this: studies show these chemicals migrate out of furniture and toys into dust that children breathe and swallow, and firefighters say the chemicals make household fires more toxic, contributing to elevated cancer rates among firefighters [S2]. The bill died where nearly every bill dies — in committee. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Children and their families, because children's products and furniture would no longer contain the ten named flame retardants and any other retardant the CPSC determines poses a substantial health risk [S2]. Firefighters also benefit, since they are exposed to toxic smoke from burning treated furniture and have pushed for these bans; the bill is named partly for them. Every household with upholstered furniture gains a lower-chemical environment. States would also gain, because the bill explicitly preserves state laws that provide stronger protection than the federal standard [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bans the manufacture, sale, distribution, and import of children's products and upholstered furniture containing ten specified chemical flame retardants, cutting the main way these chemicals enter homes [S2].

Requires the CPSC to appoint a chronic hazard advisory panel to study the health effects of all chemical flame retardants in these products, then write rules banning any others found to pose a substantial risk — closing the loophole where new replacement chemicals would otherwise appear [S2].
Does not override state laws: a state law that provides greater protection than the federal standard is not preempted, so states like California or Washington could keep or pass stricter rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical flame retardant manufacturers, whose products would be banned from a large consumer market segment, and furniture and children's product makers, who would need to reformulate products and prove compliance within roughly a year of enactment [S2] [S3]. Consumers could see small price increases as manufacturers redesign products, though the CPSC rulemaking process means most of the cost arrives after public review [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Flame retardant makers and furniture manufacturers.

drawbacks.text: Flame retardants were added to furniture for a reason: to slow the spread of fire. Removing them without adequate replacement testing could increase fire risk in some products, which is the strongest good-faith objection to a ban like this [S2].

The bill's protection arrives slowly. The CPSC must first empanel a chronic hazard advisory panel, receive its report, and then go through rulemaking before banning additional retardants — a multi-year process — meaning the ten listed chemicals are banned promptly but the broader chemical class is not [S2] [S3].
Manufacturers of furniture and children's products bear reformulation and compliance costs within about a year of enactment, costs that could be passed to consumers as modest price increases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial and long-term: removing chemicals linked in the research record to health concerns from the furniture and toys children touch every day, plus reduced toxic smoke exposure for firefighters. The costs are one-time reformulation expenses for manufacturers and a small fire-safety tradeoff in some products, and the bill itself mitigates the biggest objection by only banning named chemicals that have already been studied while requiring an expert panel review before any broader action [S2] [S3]. On the merits, the benefits to children and firefighters plausibly outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the 113th Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Schumer introduced the bill on September 15, 2014, with one cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the Commerce Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, the Senate never voted, and the full action history ends with the referral [S5].
The bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, requiring a fresh bill to be introduced in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of chemical flame retardants, who can keep selling their products in children's goods and upholstered furniture in the U.S. market. Also, indirectly, furniture and children's product makers who avoided reformulation costs. Children and firefighters ended this Congress no better protected than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Flame retardant manufacturers; no vote was ever taken.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered its framing around protection of children and firefighters.

for.name: The bill's one cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor in the 113th Congress.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee chair with authority to schedule action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee from September 2014 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Chemical flame retardant manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose products the bill would ban from a major consumer market
against.what_they_did: Opposed flame retardant restrictions, as the industry has done in past regulatory fights over these chemicals.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll-call to examine; the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats, and no senator went on record in opposition [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill bans ten of its chemicals from children's products and upholstered furniture and sets up a process to ban more, removing a major U.S. sales channel [S2]. The industry profits by selling chemicals that end up in household dust and firefighter smoke; its interest runs against the bill's health protections [S2].

Manufacturers would bear reformulation and compliance costs within about a year [S3], but they would also shed exposure to chemical-liability claims and gain products marketed without the flagged chemicals. Gains and costs roughly balance.

Firefighters face cancer risk from toxic smoke released by burning flame-retardant-treated furniture; a group named in the bill's title [S2]. Not an industry in the commercial sense, but an organized occupational group the bill would directly protect.
